games.explanation: Wesneski is the exact kind of arm right-handed lineups feast on, and Philadelphia is running out a top four that treats righties like batting practice regardless of handedness. His splits against righty bats are ugly across the board, with a barrel rate north of 14% that Schwarber and Harper are built to exploit even from the opposite side. Add in a park that plays up for power and a Phillies club the model has a comfortable edge on before you even get to the pitching mismatch, and -130 is a fair toll. The board is treating this like a coin flip with juice, when the shape of the game says otherwise.

Alcantara's name still carries weight the current version hasn't earned, and the market keeps pricing him like the Cy Young arm instead of the guy hitters are actually squaring up. Righties in particular have handled him just fine, which is a problem when you're staring down a Lindor-Soto-Bichette top three that does its best work against right-handed pitching. Manaea isn't a matching ace but he misses enough bats to keep a middling Miami lineup from running away with anything, and the sim sees a one-run game the board is treating like a coin flip tipped the wrong way. At +116 on the better team by a hundred Elo points, the price is doing the work for you.

Detmers is one of those lefties who looks fine in the aggregate until you notice righties handle him just fine, and Boston is about to run a lineup full of them at him. The Sox project as the meaningfully better team here, and the split that matters, Detmers versus right-handed bats, sits north of a .340 wOBA. Jahmai Jones in particular has been barreling lefties into orbit all year, and the rest of the order does not have to do much heavy lifting behind him. Fenway's slight run boost with the wind knocked down is exactly the environment where the better lineup grinds out the win without needing a crooked number. -136 on a team our numbers make closer to a -200 favorite is where the ticket writes itself.

Skubal against a lineup full of right-handed bats who happen to hit lefties well is a quieter matchup than the price suggests, and Cincinnati brings exactly that roster. Myers and Stephenson both jump a full tier when a southpaw shows up, Sal Stewart has been squaring balls up like he's allergic to soft contact, and even Elly's platoon split points the right direction tonight. Lodolo doesn't need to out-duel Skubal, he just needs to keep it within a swing in a hitter's park where the ball is carrying at 99 degrees. At +270 on a game our sim has landing inside a run, you're being paid heavyweight money for a middleweight underdog.

Toronto is a legitimately better team, but this line is priced like the Jays are hosting a Triple-A affiliate, and the actual pitching matchup does not cooperate with that story. José Soriano walks the ballpark and gives up hard contact to everyone, which is exactly the profile that keeps bad offenses in games they have no business being in. Our own sim has this landing inside a run, and getting a free base and a half on top of that is the entire ballgame. Jack Perkins misses bats at a 30% clip, so the blowout scenario the market is pricing needs Vlad to carry the whole thing himself. At even money on the run and a half, you are being paid to bet against a coronation.

Skubal is going to do Skubal things, but a run and a half is a lot of cushion when the Reds are also a lefty-flavored lineup that carries actual pop against righties. Elly and Stewart eat right-handed pitching, and Lodolo is a competent enough southpaw to keep this from spiraling into the blowout the price implies. The simulation has this landing inside a run, and a homer-happy park in ninety-nine degree heat isn't exactly the environment for a clean seven-inning shutdown from either side. Getting plus money on a Reds team that only needs to lose respectably is the entire pitch.
